DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2025.13.150.setting: Tertiary care children's hospital, all paediatric surgical services
DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2025.13.150.standard: ACS NSQIP-Paediatric UTI rates; project aim of a 30% reduction in paediatric perioperative UTIs within 1 year

cycle1.result: Institution's paediatric UTI rate had an odds ratio of 1.9x compared with the predicted rate (NSQIP 'Needs Improvement'); audits of catheterisation practice identified areas for improvement.

DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2025.13.150.intervention: Multidisciplinary working group; 'permissive list' of procedures for which catheters may be required; standardised early catheter removal except urological procedures; education on insertion and maintenance; standardised equipment and technique; electronic medical record order sets as a forcing function.

cycle2.result: 47% reduction in perioperative UTI rate by project completion; 96% adherence to the 'permissive lists'; NSQIP-Paediatric status improved from 'Needs Improvement' to 'Exemplary'.

DOI:10.1302/1358-992x.2025.13.150.other_findings: Implementation was delayed by COVID-19, giving a two-year project duration.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.471.topic: COVID-19 vaccine uptake in perinatal mental health patients
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.471.setting: West Kent community perinatal mental health team, Kent and Medway NHS and Social Care Partnership Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.471.standard: JCVI and RCOG guidance strongly recommending COVID-19 vaccination

cycle1.result: 59% (n = 51) had both doses, 12% (n = 10) a single dose and 29% (n = 25) were unvaccinated; 68% (n = 17) of unvaccinated patients were pregnant and 32% (n = 8) postnatal.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.471.intervention: All unvaccinated women were contacted and offered further information (RCOG information sheet and decision aid).

cycle2.result: After contact, 39% (n = 9) decided to accept the vaccine, 52% (n = 12) refused and 26% (n = 6) were uncertain but willing to consider it.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.471.other_findings: Reasons for hesitancy included lack of trust in the vaccine, concern about rapid development, side effects in close associates and scepticism about efficacy.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10359.topic: Self-harm care in the emergency department
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10359.standard: RCEM 2022 Mental Health in Emergency Departments toolkit (based on NICE and Royal College of Psychiatrists guidance): triage, observation of at-risk patients, quality of ED assessment

cycle1.result: Parallel assessments 39%; time to triage 45 minutes; time to physical health assessment 170 minutes; dedicated mental health triage 64%; well-documented physical health assessment 86%; risk assessment quality 11%; documented observations 30%; compassionate care 13%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10359.intervention: Monthly meetings with the Psychiatry Liaison Team; appointment of an ED safeguarding lead; alcohol liaison nurses twice weekly.

cycle2.result: Parallel assessments 56%; time to triage 40 minutes; time to physical health assessment 125 minutes; dedicated mental health triage 98%; well-documented physical health assessment 92%; risk assessment quality 17%; documented observations 20%; compassionate care 21%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10359.other_findings: Documented observation of at-risk patients declined and compassionate care improved only modestly; a standardised mental health proforma is planned.

DOI:10.1111/anae.15704.setting: Department of Anaesthesiology and Pain Medicine, Inselspital, Bern University Hospital
DOI:10.1111/anae.15704.standard: Institutional airway (anaesthesia pre-induction) checklist; primary outcome proportion of wholly performed checklists

cycle1.result: Checklist completed in 57.3% overall; adherence improved from 48.3% in the first year to 66.7% by the fifth year (p < 0.001).

DOI:10.1111/anae.15704.other_findings: Completion was lower at night (35.0% vs 61.3% by day), outside theatres (41.0% vs 66.8%) and in emergencies (35.4% vs 65.4%; OR 0.58, 95%CI 0.49–0.68); airway difficulties occurred in 4.2% of procedures.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.594.setting: Old Age Psychiatric Ward, Acute Medical Unit and Geriatric Ward, hospitals in Inverness
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.594.standard: Local protocols for managing distress in older adults (non-pharmacological approaches and rapid tranquilisation)

cycle1.result: Nurses consistently used non-pharmacological de-escalation before RT, in line with the local protocol; physical restraint only used where there was risk, by trained staff; junior doctors, especially in AMU, had limited understanding of the RT protocol.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.594.other_findings: Further education and training on the RT protocol for junior doctors was recommended.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.282.setting: Three local acute adult mental health wards
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.282.standard: NICE Guideline 192 (Antenatal and Postnatal Mental Health), sections 1.2 and 1.4

cycle1.result: 4 women received contraception advice (a further 8 already using contraception); impact of antipsychotics on fertility discussed with none; no women advised about preconception counselling; impact of psychotropics on future pregnancy discussed with one woman.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.282.intervention: Planned: teaching on preconception counselling, posters for wards and doctors' offices, and an information leaflet for women of childbearing age; re-audit in 6 months.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.282.other_findings: Practice fell well below the NICE standard.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znab430.128.topic: Pancreatic enzyme replacement after upper GI surgery
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znab430.128.setting: Regional centre for upper GI cancer surgery, Royal Liverpool University Hospital

cycle1.result: PERT started in 66.6% of total gastrectomies, 34.7% of subtotal gastrectomies, 22.4% of oesophagectomies and 33% of colonic interpositions; symptom improvement in 68.1% of total gastrectomy patients on PERT and 100% of subtotal gastrectomy patients.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znab430.128.other_findings: No significant weight improvement at 9-12 months with Creon started 0-3 months post-operatively (p = 0.19); effective dose averaged 50,000–75,000 units with every meal and snack.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.223.setting: Broadmoor Hospital, high secure forensic psychiatry hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.223.standard: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (including six-monthly HbA1c monitoring)

cycle1.result: Over 30 inpatients with type 2 diabetes audited across two cycles; baseline figures not reported separately.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.223.intervention: Recruitment of a dietician to the hospital.

cycle2.result: Improved adherence to six-monthly HbA1c monitoring, but fewer than 50% had HbA1c at or below target; 23 patients had documented offer of dietician referral.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.223.other_findings: High rates of obesity, dyslipidaemia and hypertension; diabetic retinopathy 8%, nephropathy 5.4%, macrovascular disease 5.4%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.472.setting: Two community treatment teams, Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.472.standard: CNTW Trust Policy and BNF prescribing guidance; compliance required 90–100% of prescriptions meeting each standard

cycle1.result: Prescribing rate 7%; documented indication 61.65%; prescriptions <4 weeks 58.2%; written advice 10.7%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.472.intervention: Previous audit cycles (2009, 2017, 2018); interventions between cycles not described.

cycle2.result: Prescribing rate 10.8%; 100% compliance with BNF limits, avoiding diazepam 10 mg and no prescribing in pregnant/post-partum women; documented indication 80.8%; prescriptions <4 weeks 79.2%; written advice 5.8%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.472.other_findings: Documentation of indication, duration and review plans ranged 31.5%–81.2%, verbal advice 0–16.9% and tapering plans 16.1%; 41/51 encounters were by telephone or video. Planned educational email, poster and quiz with re-audit in one year.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11597.topic: Psychiatric liaison service referrals and outcomes
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11597.setting: Ageless Psychiatric Liaison Service, Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Trust

cycle1.result: WAA referrals mostly crisis-driven (88% medically optimised at referral), managed by nurse-led model and mostly discharged to community services; older adults needed one-to-one nursing in nearly half, multidisciplinary input in 92%, 20% awaited psychiatric admission with transfer delays of 23 hours to 21 days.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11597.other_findings: Described as a re-audit but previous cycle results are not reported; lack of an older adult crisis pathway identified.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.011.setting: Paediatric day units, Great North Children's Hospital, Newcastle upon Tyne
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.011.standard: Local trust guidelines based on BSPAR guidance (rheumatology) and ESPGHAN guidelines (gastroenterology)

cycle1.result: 17 rheumatology and 17 age-matched Crohn's gastroenterology patients audited; specialties were not following all guidelines perfectly, particularly pre-treatment viral screening (detailed results in a table not supplied).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.011.intervention: Recommended development of cross-specialty infliximab guidance.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.011.other_findings: One child with JIA non-compliant with a second immunosuppressant had an anaphylactic reaction after the 5th dose.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11667.setting: General adult community mental health team, Southern Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11667.standard: NICE ADHD guidelines: baseline observations, 6-monthly weight, HR and BP, 6-monthly psychiatry review, side-effect assessment

cycle1.result: 9/21 (43%) lacked baseline observations; 14/21 (67%) no 6-monthly weight; 15/21 (71%) no 6-monthly HR/BP; 8/21 (38%) no 6-month psychiatry review; 1/21 (5%) letters no side-effect discussion; 10/21 not under PHMT or a key worker.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11667.intervention: Identifiable ADHD caseload created; patients referred to the Physical Health Monitoring Team; reflection on more specific side-effect documentation.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11667.other_findings: 21/31 patients with confirmed ADHD were medicated; side-effect documentation varied (48% general, 38% specific).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.303.setting: Ward 4, Becklin Centre, male working-age acute psychiatric ward
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.303.standard: AIMS assessment every 3–6 months for patients taking antipsychotics; AIMS for all on regular antipsychotics for three months or more

cycle1.result: 3/33 (9.1%) on antipsychotics >3 months had AIMS; 14 (28.0%) given verbal EPSE information; 12 (24.0%) given information on wider side effects; 19 (38.0%) had documented side-effect assessment at review.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.303.intervention: Recommended education of the medical workforce and raising awareness of TD symptoms.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.303.other_findings: Poor compliance attributed to lack of awareness of guidance.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11720.setting: Acute psychiatric inpatient service, Mount Carmel Hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11720.standard: American Society of Addiction Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline for Alcohol Withdrawal Management

cycle1.result: Alcohol use documented in 132 (70%); of 36 regular drinkers, duration of dependency and time of last drink documented in 8.3%, CIWA-A in 66.7%, previous withdrawal delirium, seizures and autonomic activation 0%; urine toxicology 63.9%, LFTs 52.8%, INR 27.8%, ethanol 36.11%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11720.intervention: Recommended a locally adapted alcohol assessment guideline and re-audit.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11720.other_findings: Comorbidities (100%), other substance use (100%) and suicide risk (91.7%) were well documented.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.46.setting: Four inpatient paediatric wards using electronic prescribing
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.46.standard: Legal prescribing requirements (Medicines Act 1968), trust Medicines Management Policy; ten standards based on RCP Generic Medical Record Keeping Standards 2017

cycle1.result: 100% compliance for most demographics and prescription items and all fluid standards; allergy status 95% (severity 93%); weight 73%; antimicrobial indication 81% and duration 46%.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.46.intervention: Results presented locally and emailed to staff; recommended e-prescribing training and compulsory weight and allergy entry.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.46.other_findings: Electronic prescribing improved adherence compared with previous paper chart audits.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.40.setting: Paediatric wards and prescribing tests for new paediatric doctors
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.40.standard: Legally and clinically correct CD TTO prescriptions on the CD TTO template

cycle1.result: 67% of prescribers failed the CD TTO test question, mostly dose and frequency errors; 50% of live CD TTOs (two audited) not on the template; average 40 minutes to triage one CD TTO.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.40.intervention: Recommended awareness of template location, teaching sessions, adding template to the back of the Child Health chart, and a pocket guide.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10599.topic: GP referrals to community mental health team
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10599.setting: Balbriggan Community Mental Health Team, Dublin

cycle1.result: 60 accepted (54.5%) and 50 rejected (45.5%); 16% not receiving psychotherapy, 11% suboptimal medication doses, 9% declined for non-initiation of medication.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10599.intervention: Local referral guidelines on appropriate referral, psychotherapy initiation and medication management shared with GPs on 19 August 2024.

cycle2.result: 71 accepted (92.2%) and 6 rejected (7.8%); 14% still not receiving psychotherapy.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10599.other_findings: Rejected ADHD/ASD assessment referrals rose from 21% to 33%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.458.setting: Male and female acute inpatient units, Zinnia Centre, Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.458.standard: BSMHFT admissions policy: pre-referral MDT assessment including senior doctor, rationale and plan of care, risk assessment, section status and bed type

cycle1.result: Assessed by full MHA team 49%, senior psychiatric doctor 34%; up-to-date assessment summary 67%; risk assessment 82%; detailed plan of care 35%; capacity assessment with outcome 13%; bed type considered 13%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.458.other_findings: Plan of care and bed type were rarely addressed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.841.topic: Pharmacological management of borderline personality disorder
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.841.standard: NICE CG78 Borderline personality disorder (eight prescribing, indication and review standards)

cycle1.result: >90% compliance for review of effectiveness and tolerability and no medium/long-term antipsychotic use; <79% for single-drug prescribing, agreeing target symptoms and duration, and written information; 80-89% for sedatives <1 week and discontinuing ineffective treatment.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.841.intervention: Planned: key cards for clinicians, written information for patients, re-audit in 6 months.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.600.setting: Acute male inpatient psychiatric ward, South London
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.600.standard: 100% of patients meeting 'Patient-Centred Prescribing' criteria (ward round discussion, written leaflets, informal discussion groups) by March 2021

cycle1.result: 30% of clients answered passively to 'Do you feel involved in your care?' in baseline patient experience data.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.600.intervention: Weekly MDT-led medication discussion groups from week 1; rolling rota and posters from week 6; patient information leaflets offered 1:1 from week 14.

cycle2.result: Median 92.86% of patients fulfilled Patient-Centred Prescribing criteria.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.600.other_findings: 79.3% of questionnaire responders wanted further sessions and 88% of Blob Tree responses suggested a positive emotional response; COVID-19 affected momentum.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11703.setting: Liaison psychiatry, University Hospital of Limerick
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11703.standard: Checklist of required data items derived from the 2025 redesigned referral form

cycle1.result: Old form showed inconsistent completion of GP details, referring doctor and contact details; cognitive screening items rarely recorded; previous diagnoses, medication and risk often missing.

cycle2.result: Redesigned form improved completeness across nearly all domains, with full compliance for patient identifiers and referrer details; risk documentation among the largest improvements.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11703.other_findings: No numerical completion rates given; challenges remain with usability of referral information.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11755.topic: Mild cognitive impairment diagnosis and management
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11755.setting: Eight older adult community mental health teams, Lincolnshire Partnership Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11755.standard: Older adult memory assessment and management service protocol, Manchester Consensus recommendations, NICE NG16 and NG97

cycle1.result: Standardised cognitive tool 100%; functional impairment 78%; depression screening 70%; medication review 10%; lifestyle advice 42%; cardiovascular advice in GP letter 21%; no antidementia prescribing; follow-up review 69%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11755.intervention: Findings shared across teams and MAMS how-to guide created with assessment checklist and patient/carer information pack; re-audit planned.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11755.other_findings: 21% diagnosis changed to dementia at follow-up; 16% offered research participation; 19% not followed up with no reason recorded.

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.081.setting: Southampton General Hospital, Major Trauma Centre

cycle1.result: Mean time to surgery 80 hours; surgical delays in 57.4%; 30-day mortality 4.7%.

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.081.intervention: Additional theatre allocation, dedicated hip fracture team, multidisciplinary medical evaluation, optimised imaging, management of pre-existing conditions and standardised anticoagulation reversal.

cycle2.result: Mean time to surgery 55 hours; delayed surgeries 63.9%; 30-day mortality 3.0% (national average 5.9%).

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.081.other_findings: Delays correlated with longer length of stay in both cycles; six deaths in each of the non-delayed (5.7%) and delayed (3.2%) groups post-intervention.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljag086.326.setting: 14 patch test centres in the UK and Ireland (British Society for Cutaneous Allergy)

cycle1.result: 156/3367 (4.6%) had at least one positive baseline rubber reaction; carba mix 2.6%, thiuram mix 1.9%; 69/612 extended rubber series tests positive.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljag086.326.other_findings: Some additives not in the baseline or rubber series were positive, suggesting underdetection; BSCA will update its rubber series.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.350.setting: Birmingham Skin Centre, Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.350.standard: 2018 British Association of Dermatologists and British Photodermatology Group PDT guidelines; clearance ≥ 75%

cycle1.result: All treatments licensed; 3-month clearance 52% (11/21 with recorded assessment); 12-month clearance 50% (2/4); no individual pain plans; patient satisfaction recorded in 9% (3/32).

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.350.intervention: Planned standardised digital referral and documentation system.
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.350.other_findings: Ambulatory vs standard PDT was not recorded; clinicians wanted PDT teaching and online referrals.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11418.setting: Eastbourne Department of Psychiatry, Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11418.standard: SPFT guidelines: 100% with date of initiation and indication recorded, consultant support for continuation, and indication, duration, dose and reducing regimen communicated to GP

cycle1.result: 12.5% regular and 15% PRN benzodiazepines on discharge; of these 80% on long-term treatment and 40% had documented indication and reducing regimen.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11418.intervention: Teaching on benzodiazepine prescribing for residents at the start of rotation.

cycle2.result: 9% regular and 0% PRN on discharge; 100% consultant supported with indication, duration and reducing regimen documented.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11418.other_findings: Re-audit covered only the male ward, limiting generalisability.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11694.setting: South West community Perinatal Mental Health Team
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11694.standard: NICE guidance: routine enquiry about alcohol use in all pregnant women

cycle1.result: Alcohol use explored in 16/35 (45.7%); not explored in 19 (54.3%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11694.intervention: Findings presented at MDT meeting in September 2025 with agreed routine enquiry and documentation using the AUDIT screening tool where appropriate.

cycle2.result: Alcohol use explored in 17/22 (77.3%); not explored in 5 (22.7%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11694.other_findings: An information leaflet on alcohol in pregnancy and breastfeeding was then introduced.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11826.setting: General adult community mental health team, Pennine Care Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11826.standard: PCFT HDAT initiation and monitoring guidelines across 8 domains; 100% compliance required

cycle1.result: Average compliance 60.6% across all domains; HDAT form completion 0%; consultant initiation 83%; 2.13% of patients on HDAT.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11826.intervention: Local HDAT register created with biannual review by resident doctors.

cycle2.result: Average compliance 77%; compliance rose in 5 domains with 100% in consent, annual review, side effects and GP notification; HDAT form 67%; consultant initiation 83%; 2.06% of patients on HDAT.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11826.other_findings: Blood tests and ECG monitoring fell (25.4% and 75.1% relative reductions); HDAT was discontinued in 50% of the baseline cohort after register review.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10550.setting: Acute adult, PICU and specialist inpatient units across 4 boroughs (Warrington, Halton, Knowsley, Wigan), Mersey Care Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10550.standard: POMH-UK Quality Improvement Programme 14c: 5 standards (12 criteria) and 3 targets for alcohol detoxification

cycle1.result: Four of twelve criteria (liver function and glucose tests, prescription for acute withdrawal, parenteral thiamine) and all three targets (breath test at admission, relapse prevention, referral to specialist alcohol services) had less than 60% compliance and were below the national sample.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10550.intervention: Recommended trust-wide guidance, a junior doctor admission checklist, induction teaching and routine admission bloods.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10550.other_findings: Second re-audit in the POMH-UK cycle, compared with 2016; practice varied across the trust.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11401.standard: NICE recommended dementia blood tests (FBC, U&Es, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c, calcium, ESR or CRP, B12/folate) within two months of referral

cycle1.result: 11.9% of referrals had all recommended blood tests; 27.1% had none.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11401.intervention: Focus groups with the memory clinic team, information update letter and updated referral proforma distributed to primary care clinicians.

cycle2.result: 85.7% of referrals used the proforma; all recommended blood tests in 23.8% overall and in 80% of proforma referrals.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11401.other_findings: 101 referrals across both cycles; memory clinic staff will now return referrals lacking up-to-date bloods to primary care.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.123.setting: 15 wards, Broadmoor Hospital, high secure forensic psychiatry hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.123.standard: Local Trust guidelines: vitamin D checked within one month of admission then three-monthly, with prescribing by level

cycle1.result: 76.4% checked within one month of admission; 66.7% checked within the last 3 months; 21.4% prescribed the correct dose, 22.9% under-dosed, 14.3% over-dosed and 41.4% given no dose where indicated.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.123.other_findings: Deficiency fell from 43.6% on admission to 14.5% on most recent level.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10289.topic: Emergency department management of self-harm in under-18s
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10289.setting: UK emergency departments, nine medical schools (SPARC student-led national audit)

cycle1.result: Nearly 500 ED records reviewed; 25% of records excluded for data quality issues. Clinical audit results not reported.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10289.other_findings: Focus is lessons on student-led audit methods; decentralised peer training gave variable knowledge transfer.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10413.standard: Bowel monitoring with Bristol stool charts and consideration of preventative laxatives for patients on antipsychotics

cycle1.result: Bowel movement recorded on 5 days in total over 2 weeks; 2 bowel charts uploaded.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10413.intervention: Bristol stool charts with staff training; charts integrated into MDT discussions with further training; then Norgine risk assessment tool and patient tutorial.

cycle2.result: 151 days recorded, average Norgine score 7.056 and all charts uploaded.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10413.other_findings: Second cycle (18 patients) recorded 173 days with 16 charts uploaded; monitoring fell 8.73% from the second to third cycle.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.851.topic: Antipsychotic physical health monitoring in CAMHS
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.851.setting: Child and Family Clinic, tier 3 outpatient CAMHS, Belfast Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.851.standard: Belfast Trust CAMHS Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring Schedule (2015), based on CAMESA, NICE CG185, CG155 and Maudsley guidelines

cycle1.result: Baseline bloods 92%; baseline ECG 75%; complete monitoring bloods 33%; physical health parameters complete 42%; schedule present and current 42% (0% on PARIS).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.851.intervention: Standardised recording using PARIS clinic letters and the schedule at the front of notes; baseline ECG mandatory.

cycle2.result: Baseline bloods 89%; baseline ECG 67%; complete monitoring bloods 44%; physical parameters complete 56%; schedule present and current 38%, present but not current 50% (0% on PARIS).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.851.other_findings: Small numbers limit interpretation; initiation checklist, bloods diary and care-pathway booklet proposed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.553.setting: West Lothian Psychiatry, district general hospital (Psychiatric 2222 call)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.553.standard: 90% documentation compliance using a new checklist

cycle1.result: Psychiatric team documentation 44%; ward nursing documentation 65%; medical ward doctor documentation 39%; appropriate calls 65%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.553.intervention: Documentation checklist in the electronic records system for completion by the junior doctor, introduced July 2023.

cycle2.result: Documentation 90%; ward nursing documentation 83%; medical ward doctor documentation 57%; appropriate calls 74%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.553.other_findings: Attending doctors staying longer than 10 minutes rose from 47% to 68%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.574.setting: Richmond and Kingston intellectual disability psychiatry caseloads
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.574.standard: Prolactin measured in the last 12 months for patients on antipsychotics and elevated results managed per current guidelines

cycle1.result: 39 (52.0%) had prolactin measured in the last 12 months; 16 (41.0%) of these were elevated; 81.3% of elevated results discussed and treatment considered.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.574.other_findings: 68.8% of those with raised prolactin were on risperidone; uptake of blood tests is the main issue.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.022.setting: Rheumatology consultant-delivered ultrasound clinic, Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: Known IA (n = 30): 43.3% active on US, 6 of 13 escalated; suspected IA (n = 30): 16.7% had US evidence of IA.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.022.other_findings: Sonographic findings were often not followed by a concordant treatment decision.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11711.standard: Medication reconciliation as a WHO safety initiative (Accreditation Canada ROP 2020 handbook): documented BPMH with ≥2 information sources

cycle1.result: 21/22 (95%) had a documented admission BPMH; 15/21 (71%) had at least one discrepancy, mostly omissions (10/17, 59%); ≥2 information sources documented in 1/21 (4.8%).

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11711.intervention: Findings shared with clinicians; DIS MedRec form with pre-populated provincial Drug Information System medication list implemented in late September 2025, with staff education.
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11711.other_findings: Pre- and post-intervention data collection (June–August 2025 vs November 2025–January 2026) is ongoing.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10673.setting: Punjab Institute of Mental Health, Lahore
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10673.standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists ECT guidelines (consent, vital signs, monitoring of clinical response and cognitive side effects)

cycle1.result: Consent forms completed 100% and ongoing consent checked for all; right to withdraw consent explained to none; vital signs robustly documented; no validated rating scale used; response between sessions assessed in 45%; no documentation of cognitive side-effect assessment.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10673.intervention: Recommended updating consent forms to include right to withdraw, culturally validated assessment tools and re-audit in one year.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.222.setting: Broadmoor Hospital, high security psychiatric hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.222.standard: NICE CG142 Autism spectrum disorder in adults: diagnosis and management

cycle1.result: 13 (76.5%) with confirmed ASD prescribed antipsychotics, nine with comorbid psychotic disorder; none prescribed psychotropics for core ASD symptoms; off-licence antipsychotic use not documented in any relevant participant in the preceding 12 months.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.222.other_findings: Suggests forensic-specific prescribing guidance may be needed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11365.setting: Acute adult mental health inpatient unit, Belfast Health and Social Care Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11365.standard: Project aim of 10% improvement in documentation of driving status and driving advice within 8 weeks

cycle1.result: Driving status documented in 48 patients (median 60%); driving advice documented for 10 of 20 drivers (median 50%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11365.intervention: Education session for resident doctors on driving regulations; poster prompt in the resident workspace; mandatory driving status field in the discharge meeting template.

cycle2.result: Driving status documented in 53 patients (median 83%) with a run chart shift; driving advice documented for 17 of 27 drivers (median 80%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11365.other_findings: Driving advice documentation varied widely week to week with several weeks of zero compliance and no run chart shift.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10338.topic: Dopamine agonist screening in gambling disorder
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10338.standard: 100% of initial assessments include a full medication history including dopamine agonists; 100% of patients on dopamine agonists screened by a psychiatrist before treatment allocation

cycle1.result: Full drug history documented in 53% (16/30); 17% (5/30) prescribed a dopamine agonist (all aripiprazole), of whom 1 was referred for psychiatrist screening.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10338.intervention: Recommended staff training and discussion with a psychiatrist where appropriate.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.419.topic: Psychotropic prescribing and monitoring in learning disability
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.419.setting: Learning disability female low secure forensic unit
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.419.standard: Trust and national prescribing and monitoring guidelines

cycle1.result: 100% compliance for indications on drug chart, care plans for combined or high-dose antipsychotics, consent to treatment forms, annual health check and psychotropic blood monitoring; MHA capacity assessment forms 71%; valproate annual risk acknowledgement forms 0%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.419.intervention: Recommended care plans for all patients on valproate with review dates for risk acknowledgement forms, and consistent filing of results.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.419.other_findings: Investigation results were difficult to locate.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11561.setting: Hamad Medical Corporation Mental Health Services

cycle1.result: PD diagnosis in 83/171 (48.5%), mostly BPD (65.1%); MDT review 86.7%; crisis plan 61.4%; zero documented individual psychotherapy sessions in 26/48 and zero group sessions in 34/51; antipsychotics 69.9% and benzodiazepines 39.8%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11561.other_findings: No local guideline exists; 59.0% were readmissions and 25.3% had inpatient self-harm.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11712.topic: Timeliness of GP letters after assessment
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11712.setting: CMHT Swords – Orange Team, North Dublin Mental Health Services
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11712.standard: NHS Standard Contract (2022) and HSE National Clinical Programme for Mental Health (2020): GP letter within 14 days of assessment

cycle1.result: 15 (75%) sent within 7 days, 4 (20%) within 8–14 days and 1 (5%) after 14 days; 95% overall compliance.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11712.other_findings: Only patients assessed by the auditor were included.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.10.standard: Local paediatric vancomycin guideline: 100% correct starting dose, 90% levels at correct time, 80% third-dose troughs in range (10–15 mg/L), 90% appropriate action for out-of-range levels

cycle1.result: 100% correct starting dose; 90% of levels taken at the correct time; 33% of initial levels in range (a further 31% after dose change); 93% appropriate actions; three of six standards met.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.10.intervention: Suggested changing dosing frequency to four times a day or continuous infusion.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.10.other_findings: Two standards could not be assessed as no neonates or renal impairment cases; 62 levels reviewed.

DOI:10.1111/anae.16388.setting: 59 UK Trusts, procedures under the care of an anaesthetist (national audit)
DOI:10.1111/anae.16388.standard: Association of Anaesthetists' 2020 consensus guideline on peri-operative glucocorticoid management

cycle1.result: Of 219 on ≥5 mg prednisolone equivalents, 67 (31%) pre-operatively and 43 (20%) postoperatively supplemented according to guideline; overall compliance 19/219 (9%); 30/219 (14%) no supplementation; 28/58 (48%) on <5 mg received inappropriate supplementation.

DOI:10.1111/anae.16388.other_findings: 21,731 operations audited; 45% of anaesthetists reported using the guideline, with adherence in only 27/125 (22%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.434.topic: Mental Health Act assessment on-call doctor involvement
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.434.standard: Local algorithm for Mental Health Act assessments: one doctor from the care team or on-call consultant in hours and one on-call doctor out of hours

cycle1.result: At least one NSCHT doctor involved in 91% of assessments (92% in the Section 136 suite, 89% out of hours).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.434.intervention: Recommended amending the Section 136 form to record the doctor's role; results presented to governance groups.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.434.other_findings: 45% detained under section 2 and 35% under section 3; substance misuse featured in 26%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10614.setting: Tri-Borough Perinatal Service (Ealing, Hounslow, Hammersmith and Fulham)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10614.standard: Service target non-attendance (DNA) rate of 15% or lower for initial assessments

cycle1.result: Overall DNA rate 35.3% (n=100), exceeding the target.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10614.other_findings: DNA rates were higher for physical centre appointments (40.0% vs 20.7% home and 25.9% remote; p=0.035) and with greater deprivation (p<0.001); ethnicity not significant (p=0.062).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.448.setting: Psychiatric Intensive Care Unit, Cheshire and Wirral Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.448.standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice: medical review within 1 hour, 4-hourly until MDT review, twice daily thereafter, with specified content

cycle1.result: 20% seen face-to-face within 1 hour; 75% seen 4-hourly until MDT review; mental health documented 97%, physical health 61%, medication 69%, rationale for continuing seclusion 72%; adverse medication effects and observation level 2%, risk to self 7%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.448.intervention: Planned presentation at junior doctor induction and a quick reference sheet before re-audit.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2023.448.other_findings: 5 seclusion episodes in 4 patients; a previous audit had not led to change.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10382.topic: Cardiometabolic assessment clinic attendance and escalation
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10382.setting: Cardiometabolic Assessment Clinic, community mental health team
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10382.standard: All invited patients should attend the CMA clinic, and all patients with concerning observations or needing signposting should be appropriately escalated

cycle1.result: DNA rate 52%; 53% of physical health issues managed correctly.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10382.intervention: Group and 1:1 staff teaching (primary care invited); information leaflet with each appointment; MEWS-based proforma for GP escalation; staff allowed to contact GP practices directly.

cycle2.result: DNA rate 42%; 90% of physical health issues managed correctly.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10382.other_findings: DNA rate remained high; domiciliary visits recommended for repeated non-attenders.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10685.setting: Two male and two female general adult inpatient wards, East Midlands
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10685.standard: Lester Tool: baseline BP, HbA1c/glucose, lipids, lifestyle review and weight within one week of initiation, then weekly weight for six weeks

cycle1.result: Baseline BP 89.5%, HbA1c/glucose 65.8%, lipids 57.9%, lifestyle review 55.3%, weight 36.8%; 5.9% had full weekly weight follow-up and 41.2% none within six weeks.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10685.intervention: Recommended awareness of baseline bloods, electronic record alerts for weekly weights and a refusal drop-down, and re-audit.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10685.other_findings: Reasons for non-compliance were poorly documented; risperidone most prescribed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11698.topic: Physical health assessment on psychiatric admission
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11698.setting: 12 general adult inpatient wards, Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11698.standard: NICE Clinical Guidelines and Trust physical health policy: physical examination and assessment within 24 hours of admission

cycle1.result: Within 24 hours: physical examination 60%, physical observations 86%, BMI 62%, MUST 62%, smoking status 54%, alcohol consumption 65%, comorbidity status 67%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11698.intervention: Recommended greater staff awareness of physical health assessment.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znad065.setting: National Oesophago-Gastric Cancer Audit, England and Wales

cycle1.result: 17 650 patients had surgery; 30-day mortality fell with audit year (OR 0.93, 95% c.i. 0.88 to 0.98) and 90-day mortality (OR 0.94, 0.91 to 0.98), with shorter postoperative stay (IRR 0.98).

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znad065.other_findings: Higher trust volume was also associated with better outcomes; little evidence of earlier diagnosis.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10538.standard: Comparison with 2024 local census ethnic composition

cycle1.result: White 90.9% of self-harm and 89.5% of ward referrals vs 91.4% census; Mixed groups absent in self-harm and 0.7% of ward referrals vs 1.3%; Asian 1.7% and 1.5% and African 0.4% and 0.8%, underrepresented.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10538.intervention: Recommended better ethnicity data collection, community outreach and cultural competency training.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11449.setting: Elm Ward, West Park Hospital, Tees, Esk and Wear Valley
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11449.standard: NICE TA77: zopiclone not exceeding four weeks including tapering

cycle1.result: Mean duration 7.7 weeks (median 8.3); 27% (6/22) within the ≤4-week limit.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11449.intervention: Practice changes introduced after the initial audit (not described).

cycle2.result: Mean duration 3.42 weeks, median 1.29 weeks; 83.3% (10/12) within ≤4 weeks; 30% of evaluable cases met indication-specific NICE durations.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11449.other_findings: Stop dates, indications, review plans and non-pharmacological interventions remained poorly documented.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11820.setting: Older adult psychiatry ward, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11820.standard: DVLA guidance on fitness to drive

cycle1.result: Driving status documented in 5 (25%) despite 18 (90%) having DVLA-relevant diagnoses; DVLA advice recorded for 3.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11820.intervention: Clinician education and prompts in the ward round template.

cycle2.result: Driving status documented in 10 (90.9%); both drivers for whom guidance applied had DVLA advice discussed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.323.setting: Psychiatry of Old Age service, North-West of Ireland
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.323.standard: NICE 2014, BNF 2019 and Maudsley 2018: 3-monthly serum lithium and renal tests, thyroid and calcium monitoring

cycle1.result: 78% (n = 14) on track for 3-monthly lithium levels; 39% (n = 7) in therapeutic range; 83% (n = 15) 3-monthly renal tests; thyroid function 89% (n = 16); calcium documented 63%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.323.other_findings: All 18 had abnormal renal function; 56% of those started by the service had renal impairment before initiation.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.148.setting: Carseview Centre (3 adult wards, IPCU and learning disability unit), NHS Tayside
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.148.standard: Local NHS Tayside Emergency Equipment Protocol

cycle1.result: Trolleys lacked ligature packs, masks not by oxygen cylinders, dextro-tablets not readily available; learning disability unit had no resuscitation trolley.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.148.intervention: Feedback to wards, multidisciplinary meetings and an updated local protocol (finalised November 2020) with recommendations.

cycle2.result: Trolleys better equipped in line with the updated protocol; missing items varied by ward but none consistent across the site; all recommendations implemented.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.148.other_findings: Additional items such as nebuliser and non-rebreather masks were stocked but hard to locate.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.569.setting: Lewisham Assessment & Liaison team (Neighbourhoods 1, 3 and 4) and GP practices

cycle1.result: Basic bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) in 54% (n = 13); glucose 38% (n = 9); prolactin 13% (n = 3); creatine kinase 0%; 0% completely monitored.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.569.other_findings: Data obtained for 24 of 40 patients; audit to be expanded to Neighbourhood 2.
